R06-G-01: Few practices in science are defended as warmly, or examined as rarely, as anonymous peer review. A manuscript arrives at a journal, an editor sends it to two or three specialists, and their verdicts, delivered without signatures, decide whether the work enters the published record. The usual defence of the anonymity is straightforward and has real force. A young researcher asked to assess a paper by the most powerful figure in her field may hesitate to point out its flaws if her name is attached to the report, since that figure may one day sit on the committee that decides her promotion. Anonymity, on this view, is what allows candour to flow upward. The trouble is that the same protection shelters other things as well. A referee who is quietly working on a rival theory, or whose own earlier results are contradicted by the manuscript, can recommend rejection without ever having to explain himself in public. Most referees, of course, do nothing of the kind; the difficulty is that nobody outside the editorial office can tell which ones do. Authors receive a verdict but not a reason they can contest, and readers never learn that a paper was turned away at all. A system designed to free the weak from the strong can thus end up freeing the established from scrutiny, because it is usually the established who are asked to referee, and a manuscript that challenges a reigning view is, by the nature of the case, most likely to be sent to the very people who hold that view. It would nevertheless be wrong to infer from all this that anonymity is, in itself, the problem. What makes it dangerous is its combination with gatekeeping power. When a referee's report merely advises, when it is published alongside the paper as one reader's criticism that the authors can answer, the identity of the critic matters far less, because the criticism must persuade on its merits. When the report decides, in secret, whether anyone will read the paper at all, the absence of a name becomes the absence of accountability. Some journals have begun to experiment along these lines, publishing papers first and attaching the referees' reports afterwards, sometimes signed and sometimes not. Such arrangements are not free of costs: they may let weak work into circulation, and they ask readers to do more of the sorting. But they reveal what the familiar arrangement conceals, namely that the case for anonymous review has always rested on an assumption about what review is for. If review exists to improve papers, a mask does little harm. If it exists to decide which papers exist, the mask deserves far more suspicion than it usually receives.
R06-G-02: Discussions of the so-called file drawer problem usually begin with journals. Editors, the complaint runs, prefer results that show something: a drug that works, an effect that appears, a difference between groups. Studies that find nothing are harder to place, and so they remain in researchers' filing cabinets while the published literature fills up with positive findings. A reader who surveys that literature will then overestimate how often, and how strongly, the effect in question occurs, since the failures that would have tempered the estimate never reached print. The literature, in other words, is not a sample of the research that was done but a selection from it, made on the very quantity that readers most want to estimate. There is truth in this account, and the remedy it suggests, journals that commit in advance to publishing well-conducted studies whatever they find, deserves the support it has received. But the account places the drawer in the wrong office. Ask a working scientist what became of her last inconclusive experiment and the answer is seldom that an editor turned it down. More often it was never written up at all. The study was abandoned before any journal had a chance to reject it, and it sits in the drawer because its own author put it there. The reason is not laziness. A positive result, whatever its other defects, announces itself: something happened. A null result is mute about its own meaning. It may show that the effect does not exist, or that the sample was too small to detect it, or that a reagent was contaminated, or that a student misread the protocol. The researcher who obtained it is often the person least able to tell which, and the most honest description she could offer, that she looked and did not see, is one that few colleagues would think worth the trouble of reading. Writing such a paper costs weeks and earns little, and the decision to move on is, from where she stands, entirely rational. If this is right, obliging journals to accept null results treats the symptom at the far end. The drawer will empty only when null results become informative, and that depends on decisions made before any data are collected: samples large enough that a real effect would probably have been seen, procedures specified in advance so that a failure cannot be blamed afterwards on improvisation, checks built in to show that the apparatus was working. A null result obtained under such conditions says something definite, and researchers will publish it for the same reason they publish anything, because it tells their colleagues something they did not know.
R06-G-03: When professional scientists first began to rely on volunteers to record birds, butterflies or the timing of spring flowers, the objection most often raised was that amateurs would make mistakes. A trained ornithologist can tell two similar warblers apart by a fragment of song; a weekend walker may not know that there are two species to distinguish. Such worries were not idle, for a single confident error repeated across many records can manufacture a trend that does not exist. Data gathered by such walkers, the argument went, would be riddled with misidentifications, and conclusions drawn from it would be built on sand. The worry was reasonable, but experience has shown it to be aimed at the lesser target. Well-run projects have learned to ask volunteers for the kinds of observation they can make reliably, such as whether any frog was heard calling at a pond on a given evening, rather than the kinds that demand years of training. Where identification is genuinely hard, volunteers can photograph what they see and leave the naming to specialists, and records that look improbable can be flagged and checked. Errors do not vanish, but when thousands of independent observations are pooled, isolated mistakes tend to be swamped by the many correct reports around them. The more stubborn problem lies not in what volunteers see but in where and when they look. People record wildlife near their homes, along popular footpaths and on fine weekends, so that their records cluster wherever leisure, access and good weather happen to coincide. They visit nature reserves more often than industrial estates, and gardens more often than farmland. A map of volunteer sightings is therefore partly a map of the species and partly a map of the observers, and no amount of skill in identification will separate the two. A bird that seems to be thriving in the suburbs may simply be living where the watchers live. This bias is harder to correct than misidentification precisely because it is invisible in any single record. Each observation may be impeccable; the distortion appears only in the pattern. Projects that take it seriously ask some volunteers to survey assigned locations at fixed times, accepting fewer and less convenient records in exchange for a sample whose shape is known. Such schemes demand more of participants, and they rarely attract the crowds that open recording does. But they show that the reliability of citizen science was never really a question about the competence of amateurs. It is a question about whether the people designing a project have thought as carefully about sampling as about skill.
R06-G-04: For much of the last century, efforts to explain science to the public rested on a simple picture. People who resisted a scientific conclusion, it was assumed, did so because they did not understand it; the gap between expert and lay opinion was a gap in knowledge, and it could be closed by supplying the missing facts. Critics later gave this picture a name, the deficit model, and the name stuck because it captured what was wrong with it: it treated the public as a vessel with a hole in it, defined entirely by what it lacked. The model fails first on its own terms. If resistance came from ignorance, those who knew most about a contested subject would be the most accepting of the expert view, yet it is easy to find people who have read widely on a topic and still reject the consensus, sometimes with more conviction than before they began. Knowledge, it turns out, can be recruited to defend a position as readily as to change it. A person who already distrusts the source of a claim does not experience new information as enlightenment; she experiences it as further pressure from that source. The facts are heard, but they are heard as moves in a contest whose sides were chosen before the conversation began. The deeper failure concerns what the model leaves out. Consider a village told by a team of engineers that a new dam upstream poses no danger. The villagers may follow the hydrology perfectly well. What they also know, and what the engineers' presentation omits, is that the last assurance they received from officials turned out to be wrong, that the benefits of the dam will flow to a distant city, and that if anything goes wrong it is they, not the engineers, who will bear the loss. Their scepticism is not a vacancy waiting to be filled. It is a judgement about whom to trust and who pays, and it may be quite rational even when the hydrology is sound. None of this means that facts are irrelevant or that every misunderstanding is secretly a stance about power. Some people do hold mistaken beliefs simply because nobody has explained a matter clearly, and for them a good explanation is exactly what is needed. The error of the deficit model was to make this the whole story. Communication that begins by asking what an audience already knows, fears and has experienced will sometimes end in explanation. But it will at least explain the right thing, and it will treat the people it addresses as parties to a decision rather than as containers for information.
R06-G-05: Generations of students have learned that science proceeds by a method, and that the method has steps. One observes, forms a hypothesis, designs an experiment, tests the hypothesis and draws a conclusion, after which the cycle begins again. The sequence is tidy, easy to examine and, as a description of what scientists actually do, very nearly useless. It is not that no scientist has ever followed it. It is that the sciences differ so widely in what they are able to do that any single recipe either excludes much of their work or becomes so general that it no longer guides anyone. Consider the range. An astronomer studying a distant star cannot intervene in it; she can only watch, and her ingenuity lies in finding natural cases that differ in just the respect she wants to compare. A geologist reconstructing how a mountain range formed is not testing a hypothesis by experiment but assembling a history from traces, much as a detective does, and her standard of success is the coherence of a narrative that accounts for scattered evidence. A laboratory chemist may indeed run controlled experiments, but she spends much of her time on something the textbook sequence ignores entirely: making instruments and procedures work at all. To call all of this 'the scientific method' is to give one name to several distinct crafts. The tidy sequence is not merely inaccurate; it does some damage. By making the controlled experiment the model of all good science, it encourages the view that sciences which cannot experiment are somehow lesser, as though reconstructing the history of the Earth were a provisional activity awaiting a proper laboratory. And by presenting science as a machine that turns hypotheses into conclusions, it leaves the public poorly prepared for the ordinary untidiness of research, in which results conflict, estimates are revised and experts disagree for long periods before they converge. People taught to expect the machine are apt to read each revision as a malfunction. Is there, then, nothing that the sciences share? There is something, but it is not a procedure. What unites the astronomer, the geologist and the chemist is a set of habits about how claims are treated once they have been made: they are exposed to colleagues who are expected to attack them, they are stated in a form that evidence could tell against, and the people who make them are expected to give them up when such evidence arrives. These are norms of a community rather than steps for an individual, and that is precisely why they cannot be captured in a flowchart. A student who had absorbed them would understand science better than one who had memorised the steps, even if she could not say in what order they come.
R06-G-06: When two researchers, one celebrated and one unknown, publish a discovery together, the discovery is very likely to be remembered as the celebrated researcher's. The same pattern appears when two people arrive at a result independently: the one who is already eminent tends to receive the larger share of the attention, the citations and the invitations that follow. Sociologists of science named this the Matthew effect, after the verse in the Gospel of Matthew about those who have being given more, and it is usually discussed as a problem of fairness. The unknown co-author did much of the work, and someone else collected the credit. That description is correct within its limits, but it understates what is at stake, and it also misses why the effect is so persistent. Scientists face a literature far larger than anyone could read in a lifetime. A familiar name on a paper is a cheap signal that the paper is probably worth the reader's time, and in a world of scarce attention, readers who rely on such signals are not being foolish. To some degree, then, the effect is the by-product of a reasonable strategy for coping with abundance. Condemning it as mere snobbery does not explain why careful and fair-minded people take part in it every day. The trouble begins when attention is converted into resources. A researcher whose papers are widely read finds it easier to win grants, which pay for students and equipment, which produce more papers, which are read more widely still. Advantage compounds. After a few rounds, the difference between two careers may bear little relation to any difference in the quality of their first ideas, and the field as a whole has placed a heavy bet on one line of work for reasons that are partly accidental. Ideas that happened to originate with the less visible researcher may wait years for a hearing, or never receive one, not because they were tested and found wanting but because nobody with the means to test them was looking in their direction. Seen in this light, the effect is less an injustice done to individuals than a distortion in how a field allocates its bets, and the remedy is not to forbid readers from noticing names, which would be both futile and costly. It is to loosen the link between attention and money: to judge some grant proposals without knowing who wrote them, to set aside funds for researchers early in their careers, and to treat a famous name as a reason to read a paper rather than as a reason to believe it.
R06-G-07: Every year, research funding agencies ask panels of scientists to read hundreds of proposals and rank them, and every year the money runs out long before the list does. The proposals near the bottom are usually easy to set aside: they are poorly argued, or unoriginal, or plainly unworkable. The difficulty lies higher up. Among the proposals that every member of the panel agrees are good, the panel must still decide which will be funded and which will not, and the line it draws often separates projects that no one present could distinguish with any confidence. It is in response to this predicament that a few agencies have begun to experiment with a once unthinkable idea: setting a threshold of quality and then choosing among the proposals above it by lot. The proposal is usually defended on grounds of efficiency. Ranking is laborious; panels spend weeks producing distinctions that a lottery would produce in minutes. This is true, but it is the weakest part of the case, and resting on it invites the reply that good decisions are worth what they cost. The stronger argument is about honesty. Experience suggests that two independent panels given the same proposals will often disagree about which of them fall just above the funding line and which just below, a sign that, near the top, the ranking reflects the composition of the panel at least as much as the merits of the work. A ranking of this kind already contains a large element of chance. What it lacks is any acknowledgement of the fact, and so its outcomes are experienced, by winners and losers alike, as verdicts on quality. Hidden chance is not neutral chance. When the members of a panel cannot tell good proposals apart on their merits, other preferences fill the gap: a taste for methods they themselves use, a wariness of projects whose payoff is uncertain, a familiarity with applicants they have met. Each of these is a mild bias, and none need be deliberate, but together they tilt the funding line toward the safe and the recognisable. A lottery among the proposals above the threshold removes this tilt at the margin. It cannot make the panel bolder, but it can stop the panel's caution from deciding cases that its judgement cannot decide. The most serious objection is not that lotteries abandon judgement, since judgement is exercised in full at the threshold, where panels are reasonably good at separating the sound from the unsound. It is that scientists need to believe that reward follows merit, and that a lottery, by announcing that it sometimes does not, will corrode the motivation on which research depends. This deserves to be taken seriously. Yet the belief it seeks to protect is, at the margin, already false, and a system that preserves morale by concealing how it works purchases that morale at the cost of misleading the very people it rewards. A researcher whose proposal loses a draw has at least been told the truth: that her work was judged fundable and that the money ran out. None of this recommends lotteries everywhere. Where proposals differ in ways that can be measured, as when an agency must choose a single design for a costly instrument, ranking is the right tool and chance would be an abdication. The argument applies only where judgement has reached its limit. Its real lesson concerns not lotteries but the pretence of precision, and agencies that decline to draw lots might still learn from it, for instance by publishing how close the decisions near their funding line actually were.
R06-G-08: A scientific paper presents itself as a complete set of instructions. Its methods section lists the materials, the quantities, the temperatures and the timings, and the implicit promise is that anyone competent who follows them will see what the authors saw. This promise underwrites one of the most cherished ideas about science: that its knowledge is public, available in principle to anyone who can read, and independent of the particular people who first produced it. When a laboratory fails to reproduce a published result, the natural suspicion therefore falls either on the original claim or on the care of the people who tried to repeat it. Anyone who has worked at a laboratory bench knows that the promise is only partly kept. Many techniques depend on skills that their practitioners cannot fully articulate: how firmly to tap a tube, how long a mixture should look cloudy before it is ready, which faint smudge on an image is signal and which is dirt. Such knowledge is not secret, and it is not mystical. It is simply of a kind that is acquired by doing and by watching others do, in the way that one learns to ride a bicycle rather than the way one learns a telephone number. A methods section can point toward it, but it cannot transmit it, any more than a manual can make its reader a competent cyclist. It is not unusual for a group trying to build a new kind of instrument from published descriptions alone to fail again and again, while another group that has sent a member to spend some weeks in the original laboratory, or has received a visitor from it, succeeds, often without being able to say afterwards what the crucial difference was. In such cases the written instructions were not wrong. They were incomplete in ways that neither their authors nor their readers could have specified in advance, because the authors did not know which of the many things they did without thinking were the things that mattered. Recognising this does not license complacency about how methods are reported. A great deal that is now left out of papers could be written down, and the habit of omitting it, whether to save space or to protect an advantage, deserves the criticism it receives. But the recognition does alter what we should expect from reform. Demanding ever longer methods sections will capture the explicit portion of a technique more fully while leaving the tacit portion exactly where it was. If the goal is that results can be checked by people other than those who produced them, some of the effort now spent on documents might be better spent on movement: on funding researchers to visit one another's laboratories, on recording procedures as they are actually performed, and on treating the training of a replicator as part of the cost of a replication. There is a larger consequence as well. The picture of scientific knowledge as a body of public statements, detachable from the people who hold it, turns out to be an idealisation. Much of what a field knows lives in the hands of its practitioners and moves only when they do. This is not a reason to distrust that knowledge, since skills can be tested by their results as surely as statements can. It is a reason to treat the communities that carry it, and the slow work of passing it on, as part of the infrastructure of science rather than as a private matter of training.
